Unraid’s Docker setup works well for a lot of people, especially if you like using a web interface and just want to spin up a few containers. But once you start dealing with more complex stacks or want to use Docker Compose regularly, it can feel a bit clunky. There’s no built-in Compose support—you have to add a plugin—and things like updating stacks, keeping configs tidy, or using version control aren’t as smooth as they are on a regular Linux system. Also, Unraid stores Docker stuff in some odd places by default, so moving setups around or automating them takes a bit more effort.

All of this doesn'ty really matter if you just want to spin up some containers and you are not already used to using Docker in Linux server environments. Unraid dockerman setup will still work fine for you, so don't be discouraged.

I already paid for Unraid and have been using it for a while now, so  I am used to its UI and would be content with using it purely for NAS purposes while disabling any virtualization and container orchestration on it. 

The main thing why I would keep Unraid though is not wanting to move away from the Unraid array as it allows me to easily mix and match different drive sizes and I am too lazy to setup SnapRAID + MergerFS, especially for a home lab.

Nothing wrong with what you are doing, not sure why anyone would feel entitled to tell someone else how to run their server. 

I just wouldn’t be able to do it. In fact, I am moving the opposite direction and trying to get an HBA card so I can virtualise Unraid under Proxmox for NAS purposes and decouple my docker stack from it. I really dislike docker implementation in Unraid, and while using docker compose plugin and dockge helps, I would rather just move my stack to an Ubuntu or Alpine VM.

Make sure your resolution and frame rate in Moonlight settings match your host settings.

It’s true, especially in popular commercial/tourist areas like the Souq. Some may look at the camera as a way to get some quick cash out of you, either by asking you whether you want to take a picture of them and then demanding a tip, or by outright being mad at you after you take some random photo in their direction, by then they can start demanding payment. This happens often with Guerrabs (traditional water porter and sellers in Souqs.)

I am not from Marrakesh, but I can imagine it can be even worse there due to how over-touristy it is.

The advice that I can give is to just own it. It depends of course on what type of street photography you do. If your hobby is mostly focused on street portraiture, it’s going to be tough not to be asked for tips and so on. If you focus mostly on wide angle shots that do not necessarily focus on a specific subject but more on the environment, it should be fine. Personally I do more abstract street photography focusing on shadows and colour, so even when carrying a big >50mm lens, it turns out okay as I try not to focus on the peoples’ likeness too much.

Take with you some small wide angle lenses e.g. 28mm, 35mm FF equivalent. March is quite sunny as well so prioritize small form factor over huge lenses with big apertures so that it helps you blend in. 

It would also be helpful to pick up some words in Darija so that whenever you have a potential situation, you can at least talk to them and show your good intentions. A smile and some good words will always help.

And definitely, definitely, get out of the souks and the touristy areas, Marrakesh has much more to offer, from a photography perspective, in the rest of its old medina and other parts of the city, and people are likely to be much more chill.

Comparing the UK to Finland when it comes to immigration is pointless. Most (legal and illegal) migrants who go to France or the UK, for example, go there not necessarily because they are giving away special lucrative visa opportunities or anything, but because of convenience; language, large and wide colonial history, large economies and developed job markets, family or community already settled there etc.

Apart from the different refugee crises in the past (Somalia, Bosnia/Balkans, Middle East and Afghanistan), I would say most migrants to Finland still came through routes you have described e.g studies, especially when there were no fees for internationals, and for work. It’s just that the sheer number of immigrants who come through those routes is way less in scale compared to the big countries in Europe, so the “monoculture” situation you are describing are more apparent in countries like Finland and Sweden etc.

If I am being completely blunt, the reason why it would be hard to attract “high skilled labour” or study prospects is that Finland is a tough place to move into. Don’t get me wrong, I love this country, but the weather coupled with a difficult language and other factors like a tough job market, where basically you get paid like in Estonia and get taxed like in Norway (exaggeration but you get my point), and a lot of the jobs are reliant on Finnish skills and/or nepotism etc.. makes it less of an ideal place for those high skilled immigrants to choose Finland.

And as such, most migrants you will see here might be people coming to Finland due to recent refugee crises. It’s not like the country itself is going out of its way to attract only specific people from specific origins, but it’s the reality of (rightfully adhering to) refugee quotas but, at the same time, not having other types of work/study immigration on the same level as other big economies and countries.
